messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Distance sampling using predefined bin size
parts:
This has minimal impact on estimation in Distance. However, you may
find that observers are no better at putting detections into 5 or 6
distance intervals than in estimating actual distances. Not sure how
many observers you will have, but laser rangefinders are quite
inexpensive, so it may be worth investing in some.

Steve Buckland

jabi zabala wrote:
> > Hello All,
> > We are developing a common bird monitoring program for a small county of some 7000 km2. We want to produce relevant information for local management, so we are planning some 250 transects on 7 different strata. However, due to field problems and other practic issues we cannot ask samplers to measure the actual distance to the bird. We are considering using some 5-6 predefined distance intervals, ask field-workers to write the numbers of individulas of each speceis detected in eahc interval, and analyze the results using program distance. I don't know how this procedure will affect the results. If someone has previous experience with similar issues, I would greatly appreciate any advice.

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: Distance sampling using predefined bin size
parts:
Depending on the meaning of your message there could be another aspect
to your question that Steve did not address. Steve addressed the use of
distance bins versus measuring a more exact distance. However, he
presumed that you intended to record a bin and a group size for each
bird sighting. But as you have written your message it sounds like you
are only going to record a cumulative count of birds of each species in
each bin which would lose the information about individual sightings.
Can you clarify your meaning here?

--jeff

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: Distance sampling using predefined bin size
parts:
Thanks for the clarification. Your original message didn't say anything
about a breeding bird survey but not being a bird biologist that would
probably have been lost on me anyhow. But also, given that this list is
read by many different folks it is important to be clear. I didn't want
anyone to interpret this to mean that they didn't need to record group
size unless most are singles and just a few pairs are encountered. I
have seen examples where people have done as you said and the group size
varied substantially and the information was lost.

If the sightings are only single birds then you are fine but if you have
a mix of singles and pairs, then these should be recorded separately or
your variance estimate for detection is not valid because the code will
treat a group of 2 birds as 2 separate sightings of single birds. This
will tend to underestimate the variance and the impact will depend on
how many pairs you see relative to singles and the relative importance
of the detection variance relative to the encounter variance. If you
have a sufficient number of lines/points (per stratum) you could use a
bootstrap to obtain a better variance estimate.

regards--jeff
